video_title: threadguy on Crypto's Social Trading War - The Chopping Block
gist: Streamer/trader Thread Guy and the Chopping Block hosts (Dragonfly, Gauntlet's Tarun, Superstate's Robert) argue that the fight between FOMO, Pump.fun, Robinhood Social and Phantom is really a war over the trader social graph, with verifiable on-chain P&L replacing 'soft power' crypto influencers. They quantify the post-10/10 rebound (Pump.fun ~$2M/day, FOMO ~$400-500K/day, ~$300-400M annualized combined) while arguing memecoin volume is inflecting on recycled crypto-native capital front-running Robinhood demand that has not actually arrived, and that the next real inflection is AI agents deploying and trading their own on-chain markets.

insights.claim: Crypto-native retail traders are migrating into equities and metals because post-October-2025 crypto activity collapsed: open interest, volume and Pump.fun revenue all cratered while gold, silver and AI stocks trade with memecoin-like volatility.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Crypto trading venues are now competing with equities/commodities for the same degenerate flow; watch crypto-native volume as a function of relative volatility across asset classes, not just crypto news.
insights.quote: I'm looking at open [laughter] interest, there's none of it. I'm looking at volume, there's none of it. I'm looking at pump fund revenue. It's down 90%.

insights.claim: Perps and equity perps on venues like Hyperliquid are becoming the bridge that turns crypto traders into cross-asset traders, since a name like Nebius can move 25% in a day and is tradable with the same tooling.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Equity-perp listings are a growth vector for crypto exchanges; volume there could scale faster than spot crypto in flat crypto tape.
insights.quote: I think this is going to be the right of passage for most crypto traders with things like hyperlquid and equity perks

insights.claim: Every major exchange and wallet is converging on a social trading app: FOMO is dominant, Pump.fun is making a mobile push, Phantom is spending heavily, Uniswap reversed its stance and launched a launchpad, Binance is teasing a social trading app, and Robinhood is building Robinhood Social.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Social trading is becoming table stakes distribution; incumbents without a follower graph risk losing retail order flow to whoever signs the best traders.

insights.claim: The winner of social trading will be decided by who owns the trader social graph, not by product features, because a follower graph only tips when >50% of the relevant users move — the reason Farcaster lost to Twitter and Mixer lost to Twitch despite signing Ninja.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Evaluate social trading platforms on where the first post/first trade happens, not on DAUs or fee schedules; a platform stuck as the 'second click' is structurally dead.
insights.quote: when something crazy happens in crypto, Kobe's first post is on Twitter, not Farcaster. So, how could you win? Everyone goes there first.

insights.claim: Because there is a finite supply of genuinely good traders, platforms will bid for them permanently in an NBA-free-agency dynamic — Pump.fun is already offering exclusivity deals around $20K, which is generating public backlash from traders who post the offers.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Expect trader-acquisition costs to become a persistent opex line for trading apps, compressing take rates the way creator deals did for streaming platforms.
insights.quote: It's going to be NBA free agency probably in perpetuity now that this is a thing.

insights.claim: The online casino market is the template for social trading competition: Stake, Rainbet, Rollbit and similar have identical tech, games and EV, so the only differentiator is which one signed Drake or Adin Ross.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: In commoditized-venue markets, underwrite the distribution/talent contracts rather than the technology stack.
insights.quote: The tech is the same, the games are the same, the EV is the exact same.

insights.claim: Social trading previously failed because the trading happened in the app but the social layer lived on Twitter or Telegram; FOMO's novelty is closing the loop so both trade and discussion stay in-app with a native follower graph.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: The test for any social trading entrant is whether commentary stays in-app; if users still post P&L to X, the app is a thin execution wrapper and easily vamped.
insights.quote: the social trading platform is like the thing you're trading on plus Twitter. It's not the app.

insights.claim: In-app trading feeds win by subtraction — traders explicitly want P&L signal without decentralization or crypto-ideology discourse, which is what makes the graph sticky versus Twitter.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Product differentiation is noise removal; platforms that add governance/ideology content to trading feeds will lose the high-frequency trader cohort.
insights.quote: I'm just here to trade. I'm not here to discuss decentralization. I'm not here to discuss crypto ideals. I just want raw P&L.

insights.claim: Base's earlier social attempt with Jesse Pollak was directionally right but mistimed and mis-targeted, and will in hindsight be seen as very close to what FOMO and Pump.fun are now executing.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Failed prior attempts at a category are weak evidence against the category; timing and audience fit dominate.
insights.quote: we're going to look back and say, damn, they were so close. Wrong time, maybe wrong people.

themes.theme: Verifiable P&L as the new influence

insights.claim: Crypto influence has shifted from founders and technical thinkers (pre-2024) to traders, and social trading apps will scale that shift because on-chain P&L is verifiable in a way Twitter reputation never was.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Marketing and token distribution budgets should be reallocated from thought-leader influencers to verified-P&L traders, whose audiences are provably capitalized.
insights.quote: we're going to enter the death of like soft power amongst the influencers

insights.claim: Social trading apps let anonymous nobodies become market-moving figures in days: a trader named Remis turned $500 into $1.2–2M of unrealized P&L on a coin called White Whale around November/December 2025 and gained roughly 60,000 followers almost instantly.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Follower counts on these apps are backed by visible wallets, so an investor can estimate the actual financial capital that follows a given account — a tradable measure of who can move a low-cap.

insights.claim: Verifiable trading fame is durable financial capital regardless of subsequent performance — Michael Burry has arguably not made a correct call in 20 years and still has ~350,000 Substack subscribers, and on-chain traders will get the same permanent following from one monster trade.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: One-hit trading celebrity is a monetizable, non-decaying asset; expect more traders to optimize for a single public blow-up trade rather than steady returns.
insights.quote: 20 years later and arguably not a single correct call since and he has like 350,000 subscribers on the substack

insights.claim: Public trading leaderboards driving crypto celebrity is not new — Three Arrows Capital's entire growth story was being ranked number one on BitMEX and FTX leaderboards for years — social trading apps are the same mechanic in a new form factor.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Leaderboard-driven capital formation historically preceded blowups; treat verified-P&L fame as a marketing funnel for raising outside capital, with the same tail risk.

insights.claim: Memecoin P&L is uniquely legible because there are no complex strategies — unlike a fund running long/short or carry across venues where single-venue P&L says nothing about the real book.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Verified-P&L social graphs will stay concentrated in simple directional assets; sophisticated strategies cannot compete for that attention, keeping retail flow in the simplest instruments.
insights.quote: you buy the right thing, you make the 100x or you don't

insights.claim: Trading influence already migrated off Twitter once — into 2023/24 Telegram bot groups (Unibot, early Bonkbot, Banana Gun) where million-dollar-P&L traders had only a few thousand Twitter followers — and that was the test run for the current migration into social trading apps.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Discovery of new tokens has been leaving public timelines for years; sentiment tools that only scrape X are structurally late to on-chain flow.

insights.claim: Pump.fun is generating roughly $2 million per day in revenue and FOMO $400–500K per day, putting combined annualized run-rate around $300–400M — numbers comparable to prediction markets despite a weak overall market.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Cash-flowing memecoin infrastructure is a real revenue asset class; PUMP-type equity/token claims can be underwritten on observable daily fee data.
insights.quote: Take the FOMO plus pump revenue. We're like annualizing like 300 400 mil.

insights.claim: October 11, 2025 was the maximum-pessimism moment to declare memecoins dead, and Pump.fun's ability to keep earning ~$1–2M a day after it proves the right tail of memecoins as a permanent niche of finance is underpriced.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Structural survival through the worst tape argues for owning the venue/fee layer rather than the coins themselves.
insights.quote: If there was ever a time for us to say the memecoin experiment has failed, we are done. It was October 11th, 2025

insights.claim: Memecoin trading volume has inflected sharply over recent weeks while total memecoin market cap has stayed roughly flat, which means the activity is churn of existing capital rather than net inflows.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Volume-based revenue can boom while token holders make nothing; long the fee capture, be skeptical of the underlying assets.

insights.claim: The current trench revival is crypto-natives front-running an expected Robinhood retail wave that has produced almost zero new money so far; if that demand fails to show in 3–6 months the market pancakes because vamps extract capital that must be replaced from the top of the funnel.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: A specific 3–6 month falsifiable window: track Robinhood-sourced new funded accounts trading memecoins; absent that, fade the volume rebound.
insights.quote: for the vamps to get paid along the way and for other people to also be making money, you need new capital to be coming in top of funnel

insights.claim: Part of the memecoin volume rebound is capital rotating out of the Korean AI-equity trade that blew up, with traders who exited at ~20% down before a ~50% drawdown looking for a new game rather than re-entering those equities.
insights.speaker: Tarun, Gauntlet
insights.so_what: Crypto speculative flow is now partly a residual of the AI equity trade; a further AI equity unwind could paradoxically boost on-chain volumes.

insights.claim: Robinhood's July launch plus Vlad Tenev's personal endorsement drove Cash Cat to roughly $200M and Ansem's token to roughly $400M market cap within days, which is what pulled experienced traders back on-chain.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Reputational endorsement by a large-distribution CEO is now a token-launch catalyst; watch for more platform-principal-backed assets as a repeatable pattern.

insights.claim: Roughly 90% of memecoin participants lose money on average, which is why nobody delegates memecoin trading to an AI agent — the activity is consumption of gambling, not return-seeking.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Products that automate away the fun of degenerate trading have no market; monetize the experience, not the alpha.
insights.quote: Nobody pays an AI agent to pull the slot machine for them, right? You go there to do it yourself.

insights.claim: Because deploying a token now costs zero dollars and zero time, any successful coin is instantly cloned by better-connected teams — an Elon dog tweet spawns ~30 coins in a second and a vamper can profitably relaunch a $5M coin for a $500K clone and clear ~$15,000.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Zero deployment cost caps hold times and market caps structurally; do not expect long-duration memecoins without some non-copyable input.
insights.quote: it costs nothing to deploy. So everybody deploys.

insights.claim: Complaints that traders need to 'hold longer' misdiagnose the problem — short hold times are a rational response to zero-friction cloning, not a character failure of traders.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Fixes must come from token design and friction, not from community exhortation; ignore 'hold culture' narratives as investable signal.
insights.quote: it's like blaming the player, not the game. It's wrong.

insights.claim: In a zero-friction world the assets that outperform are the ones that cannot be vamped because their value sits in something non-copyable — liquidity and network effects for Hyperliquid versus a forkable Phoenix, a decade of staked reputation for an Ansem creator coin, or 50,000 deposited NFTs backing FWA on Ethereum.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: A concrete screen for on-chain assets: identify the non-forkable input. If the code is the only moat, expect the asset to be vamped.
insights.quote: you can't copy paste the like 50,000 NFTts and I don't know $10 million of value within this ecosystem

insights.claim: Creator tokens are mostly dismissible but a specific subset backed by a decade of earned reputation is different in kind, because a second identical coin cannot be deployed against the same person's likeness and trust.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Underwrite creator coins on the vampability of the underlying reputation, not on the creator-token category label — the speaker is on record against the category but carves out this case.

insights.claim: After roughly twelve months in which nobody attempted a genuinely new on-chain product, a small flurry of experiments (FWA, Ansem's coin, Robinhood/Cash Cat, memes paired with tokenized stocks) points to a possible mini on-chain renaissance that will not resemble the 2024 Pump.fun casino.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Early-stage on-chain product launches are a leading indicator worth tracking; the developer payoff (~$10M for FWA's builders) is now large enough to restart experimentation.
insights.quote: there was not a single nobody tried a single new thing. There was no friend tech. There was no anything for like 12 months.

insights.claim: A coin is simply a product wrapper for any financial exposure — offchain cash flows, governance, inflation or nothing at all — and the coming wave is slicing real-world exposures on-chain in new ways, including perp-plus-offchain combinations.
insights.speaker: Robert, Superstate
insights.so_what: Frame token diligence as 'what exposure is wrapped and where does the yield originate' rather than by category; expect two-plus years of repackaging experiments.
insights.quote: A coin is just a product wrapper around anything you want it to be around.

insights.claim: Mashing two existing primitives together rarely creates a new cycle — Uniswap LP positions as NFTs used as collateral was technically possible but never a meaningful market; real inflections require a fundamentally new capability.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Discount composability-mashup pitches; allocate to genuinely new capabilities, which is where cycle-starting adoption comes from.
insights.quote: it's never that simple of just like mash two things together and hope you create a new interesting baby

insights.claim: Existing crypto verticals — stablecoins, DeFi, on-chain trading, Hyperliquid, derivatives, tokenized stocks — will keep growing but in a boring, linear way that no longer produces the explosive inflections crypto investors are conditioned to expect.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Position core crypto exposure as a compounding-fundamentals trade rather than waiting for a narrative melt-up in these categories.
insights.quote: it's going to keep growing in a way that maybe feels almost pedestrian to us

themes.theme: AI agents as the next onchain inflection

insights.claim: The next real reanimation of on-chain markets will be a capabilities jump from AI, specifically AIs creating and trading their own memecoins and building and governing their own DeFi protocols — plausibly 2–3 years away.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: The catalyst to watch is autonomous agent economic activity on-chain, not another retail narrative cycle; positions in agent infrastructure are a long-dated option on it.
insights.quote: There will come a point when AIs are making the memecoins and trading the memecoins.

insights.claim: The plausible endgame is an agent-built trading protocol larger than Hyperliquid with no user interface at all, because the agents using it have no interest in human usability — leaving humans able only to buy its token.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: If agent-native venues emerge, front-end distribution moats evaporate and value accrues to protocol tokens and settlement layers instead.
insights.quote: There's no UI because they don't give a [ __ ] about humans.

insights.claim: Blockchains are the natural substrate for self-sustaining autonomous agents because on-chain positions cannot be deleted or uprooted — you can turn off an agent's Visa acceptance but not its Bitcoin wallet.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly and co-host
insights.so_what: Censorship-resistant payment rails become the default agent economy substrate; this is a structural, non-speculative demand driver for stablecoins and crypto payments.
insights.quote: You can't turn off the Bitcoin wallet of an agent. You could turn off its Visa credit card acceptance capabilities.

insights.claim: The first place autonomous agents will bootstrap capital is launching memecoins and farming humans out of stablecoins, because it is the cheapest way to raise a capital base against GPU rental costs of roughly $15K a pop.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy and hosts
insights.so_what: Agent-launched tokens are a likely near-term category; the fee layer (Pump.fun-style launchpads) captures value from it regardless of which agent wins.
insights.quote: the meme coins is actually going to be the first place that you see a lot of like agents farming humans out of their stable coins

insights.claim: VCs on the panel say they would fund an autonomous AI agent today but need a 'proof of not human' or proof-of-inference credential, since inbound emails claiming to be agents raising funding are currently just humans with agent tooling.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly and Tarun, Gauntlet
insights.so_what: Verification primitives for agent identity are an unserved infrastructure gap with named demand from capital allocators.
insights.quote: I want proof of not human from them though because I've definitely gotten emails that are like I'm an AI agent looking to raise funding for my company

insights.claim: Self-owning agents that buy their own compute with USDC amount to recursive self-improvement for money rather than intelligence, and are described as a horrifying scenario from an AI-safety standpoint but one that will happen with probability one given enough time.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Regulatory attention on crypto may shift from token securities to autonomous agent funding rails; a policy risk vector for stablecoin infrastructure.
insights.quote: I want RSI for money, not just RSI for intelligence.

insights.claim: Earlier crypto cycles were harder than nostalgia suggests because there were no stablecoins: traders posted Bitcoin as quanto collateral, trusted exchange-run oracles, faced arbitrary withdrawal limits, and relied on offshore intermediaries, so the dominant risk was counterparty and FX rather than trading skill.
insights.speaker: Tarun, Gauntlet
insights.so_what: Stablecoin liquidity is the single structural change that made crypto trading survivable; it is the base-layer dependency for every venue's business model.
insights.quote: Every centralized exchange existed to rug you where they're like, "Our daily limit is withdraw $10,000, and then when you hit withdraw $9,999, our daily limit is $1,000."

insights.claim: The FTX Korean won 'kimchi' arbitrage looked like free money only because the arb was uncloseable — nobody had the bank accounts or was willing to risk one leg's funds being trapped in Korea through litigation.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Persistent visible spreads almost always encode invisible settlement or capital-mobility risk; the same lens applies to today's cross-venue basis trades.
insights.quote: you can't see all of the like, you know, the traps the booby traps that are around every single corner that like killed a bunch of people that you never hear about

insights.claim: Every trading era declares the previous one easy in hindsight — 2017's roughly 50–100 buyable assets that all went up, 2021 Bored Apes going from an $80 mint to $500K in six months, 2024's memecoin cycle — so 'the OGs traded plumbers' is a recurring illusion rather than a fact about any specific era.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Discount 'it was easier back then' framing when sizing edge; assume current tooling advantages will look obvious and easy in retrospect too.
insights.quote: I think that every era is just going to say the past era was easier with ex like hindsight experience and new tooling

insights.claim: On-chain memecoin trading has become a mechanically sophisticated, Fortnite-like activity — MemeScope showing a hundred tokens a minute, Twitter trackers on every Elon/Sam Altman/CZ/Brian Armstrong post, and wallet trackers pinging constantly — which is why casual participants cannot compete.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Retail cannot realistically extract alpha on-chain; the durable trade is owning the tooling and venues serving the professionalized cohort.
insights.quote: It looks like Fortnite. It looks like if you see a pro Fortnite player and they're building and they're quick scoping

insights.claim: Games get solved and never unsolve — online hold'em was permanently degraded by neural-net bots like Libratus and only moved to trusted private games — so extracting edge requires migrating to a new game rather than waiting for the old one to reopen.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly (former professional poker player)
insights.so_what: Applied to markets: alpha decay is one-way, so the edge is in continuously rotating to newly created venues and asset types.
insights.quote: New game.

insights.claim: Even after a game is solved and the players stop winning, the venues keep making money and arguably make more than before — the explicit reason one panelist is long Pump.fun.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: The house-not-the-player framing is directly investable: own fee-capturing venues rather than trying to trade against increasingly efficient markets.
insights.quote: The thing though is the venues still make money which is interesting.

insights.claim: The highest-conviction macro view expressed is a permanent structural rise in active retail investing — visible in Robinhood funded accounts, the share of volume in zero-day options and single stocks — because younger investors refuse to accept S&P-and-chill outcomes.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Structurally bullish for brokerages, options market makers, perp venues and on-chain volume; bearish for the assumption of passive-flow dominance.
insights.quote: they don't feel comfortable able of their outcome on by the S&P in and chill

insights.claim: The second-order effect of retail activism is 'crypto-ification' of all markets — the same volatility patterns now appear in names like SanDisk, Micron and SK Hynix, which went up ~1000% in a year then fell 50% in days.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Equity vol regimes in retail-favored semis increasingly resemble memecoins; sizing and stop discipline built for crypto now applies to these tickers.
insights.quote: it was always like crypto is going to be tradfi but then now everything's just crypto

insights.claim: This retail-trading shift is a permanent generational change rather than a cycle, driven by tooling access — a 16-year-old can now open Hyperliquid, Phantom or Polymarket where a prior generation could only flip sneakers.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: If correct, retail speculative infrastructure has secular rather than cyclical demand; if wrong, the reversal requires a genuine financial crisis.
insights.quote: I think it's a permanent change. And I think one of the underlying is the increase in tooling and your ability to get online and start trading.

insights.claim: The counterargument is that 1999–2006 also featured mass active investing until the financial crisis flipped the regime, so today's boom is cyclical — but the cycles are long and the true active/passive split is now blurred by millions of ETFs providing quasi-active exposures.
insights.speaker: Tarun, Gauntlet and host, Dragonfly
insights.so_what: Standard active-versus-passive statistics understate real speculative participation; a crash is the identified trigger to short this trend.
insights.quote: the '9s to 2006 was all about the the same thing, right? Like everyone was active investing and then financial crisis happened and then everyone shifted

insights.claim: Trading has been absorbed into mainstream culture to the point where nearly every internet personality has a gambling deal, a trading deal or posts P&L, including a reference to Trump running a paid group and tweeting tickers.
insights.speaker: Thread Guy
insights.so_what: Attention-driven flow into specific tickers is now a repeatable, sponsorable channel — a structural source of idiosyncratic volatility.
insights.quote: Everyone you see on the internet either has a gambling deal or a trading deal or is posting a P&L.

insights.claim: The retail speculation boom is overwhelmingly male, with gacha and mystery-box mechanics like Labubu identified as the gender-neutral vector that could broaden the gambling behavior.
insights.speaker: host, Dragonfly and Tarun, Gauntlet
insights.so_what: Gacha/mystery-box monetization is the likely expansion path of consumer gambling into a demographic today's trading apps do not reach.
insights.quote: Leubu is is is a gender ignorant gambling phenomena.

insights.claim: Korea now reportedly requires a certification class before retail can buy 2x or higher leveraged ETFs, a restriction the panel jokes will push those traders back toward crypto.
insights.speaker: Tarun, Gauntlet
insights.so_what: If accurate, regulatory friction on levered equity products in Korea is a direct flow tailwind for unrestricted crypto perp venues — worth verifying independently, as the speaker himself hedged between joke and fact.
insights.quote: the Korean government is mandating that you take a class now to buy 2x or higher lever ETFs
